title: Strongly correlated quantum matter: t--J model, real-space pairing, spin-dependent masses, and atomicity in chemical bond and nanosystems
abstract: I critically overview my research on strongly correlated fermion systems for almost five decades. It concentrated on: (i) the first derivation of what is now called the t--J model, comprising both the limit of Anderson kinetic exchange of spin--spin interaction in the Mott--Hubbard insulator and taking into account real-space pairing, subsequently applied to high-temperature superconductivity; (ii) the concept of spin-dependent heavy mass of quasiparticles in heavy-fermion systems, and (iii) the first nontrivial model of statistical thermodynamics of the Mott--Hubbard transition. Those three features, together with the specific quantum critical phenomena provide, in my view, fundamental components of the theory of strongly correlated fermions established in the 1960s. Some related questions such as introduction of atomicity in the chemical bonding (iv), and specific properties of correlated nanosystems within the rigorous EDABI (v) approach are also briefly elaborated at the end.
summary: This paper provides a critical overview of strongly correlated fermion systems, centering on the $t$-$J$ model derived from the Hubbard Hamiltonian. It details advanced theoretical techniques like canonical perturbation expansion to derive effective Hamiltonians governing high-temperature superconductivity and heavy fermion behavior. Furthermore, it extends its scope by introducing 'atomicity' as a necessary correction for describing chemical bonding in molecules.
main_problem: The central problem is developing a comprehensive theory for strongly correlated fermion systems, particularly addressing high-temperature superconductivity and understanding the nature of chemical bonding in nanosystems.
main_result: The paper establishes the $t$-$J$ model as a fundamental framework by deriving an effective Hamiltonian through canonical perturbation expansion, while also introducing 'atomicity' to correct physical descriptions of molecular bonding.
method: The methodology combines theoretical derivations using projection operators ($P_1, P_2$) on the Hubbard model, canonical perturbation theory, and analytical solutions for molecular Hamiltonians (Heitler-London type).
model_or_system: The primary models are the Hubbard/t-J model for solid-state physics (cuprates, heavy fermions) and the extended Heitler-London model for diatomic molecules like H2. The analysis spans from lattice dynamics to molecular bonding.
key_observables: Superconducting pairing correlations ($\langle \hat{b}^\dagger_{ij} angle$), spin-dependent effective masses, Mott transition behavior, Covalency, Ionicity, and Atomicity in chemical bonds.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on the strong correlation limit ($|t_{ij}| \ll U-K$) and the use of orthogonal projection operators to decompose the Fock space.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the Brillouin zone for a quantum Fermi liquid. Figure 18 shows electron density profiles for H2 at various interatomic distances, demonstrating the separation into atomic states as distance increases.
paper_structure: The structure moves from reviewing the historical development of strong correlation theory (Mott to t-J model) via Hamiltonian decomposition and perturbation expansion, to applying these concepts to specific physical regimes like superconductivity, and finally extending the formalism to analyze chemical bonding using the concept of atomicity.
why_interesting: The paper bridges solid-state physics (Hubbard/t-J models for high-$T_c$) with molecular physics ($	ext{H}_2$ bonding), providing a unified theoretical framework that addresses how correlation effects manifest differently in extended solids versus simple molecules. The concept of 'atomicity' is a novel diagnostic tool.
